# Tools and alternatives

Every tool Lorefern names is scored here with the shared method (six criteria, an evidence line for each, closeness to the paid reference, a plain recommendation by user type). Scores are judgements from sources and our own adapter work on the date shown, not benchmarks. Anything not run against the real vendor says so. No price figures are quoted because none were read from a vendor page today.

<!-- SCORES:START (generated by tools/score_tools.py, do not edit by hand) -->

Scores dated 2026-11-23. Judgements from sources and our own adapter work on the date shown, not benchmarks. A tool marked not run was scored from its description only, and a source marked not fetched was not read.

### Where the company writes things down (wiki or notes tool)

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Notion | paid | 80 | 60 | 80 | 50 | 45 | 55 | **66.5** | reference |
| Docmost | open_source | 70 | 55 | 65 | 90 | 100 | 30 | **69.0** | 88 percent of Notion |
| Outline | open_source | 75 | 45 | 75 | 75 | 95 | 30 | **68.0** | 94 percent of Notion |
| Wiki.js | open_source | 65 | 65 | 65 | 95 | 100 | 55 | **72.0** | 81 percent of Notion |
| BookStack | open_source | 60 | 65 | 80 | 95 | 100 | 30 | **70.0** | 75 percent of Notion |
| Plain Markdown folder (the template) | open_source | 70 | 85 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **85.8** | 88 percent of Notion |

What Lorefern has for each: Notion: Read only adapter tested against a stand in (not run against Notion); Docmost: No adapter. Export to Markdown into the folder (not run); Outline: No adapter. Export to Markdown into the folder (not run); Wiki.js: No adapter. Folder or Git sync into the company folder (not run); BookStack: No adapter. Export to Markdown into the folder (not run); Plain Markdown folder (the template): Built and tested. The default and the demo knowledge base (run in the tests and the demo).

**Evidence, Notion**

- Fit (80): Where many small companies already keep documents, so Lorefern meets them there.
- Setup effort (60): Needs an integration token and each page shared with it. Judged from the steps, not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): Mature hosted service with a stable public API.
- Cost (50): Seat pricing. No figures quoted, read the price page.
- Data control (45): Data sits with the vendor. Notion permissions are not copied into Lorefern tags.
- Integration depth (55): Adapter reads pages as text only. Databases and comments are not read.
- Sources: https://developers.notion.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Docmost**

- Fit (70): Self hosted wiki with spaces and pages. Close to Notion for plain documents, without its databases.
- Setup effort (55): Needs Docker and a database. Setup judged from its description, not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (65): Younger project, so expect faster change. Not tested here.
- Cost (90): Free to run. You pay for the server.
- Data control (100): Documents stay on your server.
- Integration depth (30): No adapter here. Markdown export into the company folder is the tested route.
- Sources: https://docmost.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Outline**

- Fit (75): Team wiki with a clean editor, close to Notion for written knowledge.
- Setup effort (45): Needs a database, file storage and a sign in provider to run yourself. Judged, not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): Active project with a hosted edition and a self hosted one.
- Cost (75): Self hosting is free in licence terms of the source, but check its current licence yourself.
- Data control (95): Self hosted keeps data with you.
- Integration depth (30): No adapter here. Use the Markdown export.
- Sources: https://www.getoutline.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Wiki.js**

- Fit (65): A wiki that can keep pages as Markdown files in Git, which is exactly what Lorefern reads.
- Setup effort (65): Docker image and a database. Judged from its description, not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (65): Long lived project. Its next major version was in progress when last checked from memory.
- Cost (95): Free to run. Judged from its description.
- Data control (100): Pages stay on your server, or in your Git repository.
- Integration depth (55): Git storage means the company folder can simply be its checkout.
- Sources: https://js.wiki/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, BookStack**

- Fit (60): Books, chapters and pages. Good for procedures, less flexible than Notion.
- Setup effort (65): A PHP application with a database. Judged, not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): Steady, long lived project with regular releases.
- Cost (95): Free to run. Judged from its description.
- Data control (100): Everything stays on your server.
- Integration depth (30): No adapter here. Use the Markdown export.
- Sources: https://www.bookstackapp.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Plain Markdown folder (the template)**

- Fit (70): Every document has an owner, a review date and a visibility tag in plain text. Fits what Lorefern checks.
- Setup effort (85): Copy the folder, fill it in. No account.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Plain files do not break. Someone must keep them current.
- Cost (100): Free. Judged from its description.
- Data control (100): Files stay where you keep them.
- Integration depth (100): Read directly, with a checker for the structure.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/lorefern (checked this repo)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Keep writing where the team already writes. If there is no place yet, start with the plain folder template in this repo: it needs no account and Lorefern reads it directly.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Notion has a read only adapter here that was tested against a local stand in, not against Notion. For Docmost, Outline, Wiki.js or BookStack, export to Markdown into the company folder and let Lorefern read the folder. That path is tested.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** A Markdown folder in Git costs nothing. Docmost, Outline, Wiki.js and BookStack are open source and cost a small server. Notion has its own price page; read it yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** Open source wikis are the right call when the client wants documents on their own server or the team can run Docker. They are the wrong call when the team already lives in Notion and will not move.

### Shared file storage

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google Drive | paid | 80 | 50 | 85 | 60 | 45 | 55 | **67.2** | reference |
| Nextcloud | open_source | 65 | 45 | 70 | 90 | 100 | 40 | **67.5** | 81 percent of Google Drive |
| Plain synced folder | open_source | 55 | 90 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **81.2** | 69 percent of Google Drive |

What Lorefern has for each: Google Drive: Read only adapter tested against a stand in (not run against Google); Nextcloud: No adapter. Sync a folder and read it as the company folder (not run); Plain synced folder: Built and tested (run in the tests and the demo).

**Evidence, Google Drive**

- Fit (80): Where many companies keep documents. Lorefern reads Google Docs as text and ordinary files.
- Setup effort (50): Needs a Google Cloud project, the Drive API and a service account, then sharing a folder with it. Judged, not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Mature, widely used service.
- Cost (60): Free storage tiers exist and paid plans have their own page. No figures quoted.
- Data control (45): Data sits with Google. Drive permissions are not copied into Lorefern tags.
- Integration depth (55): Read only. Comments, revisions and shared drives are not read.
- Sources: https://developers.google.com/drive/api (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Nextcloud**

- Fit (65): Self hosted file storage with sync clients. A synced folder is what Lorefern reads.
- Setup effort (45): A PHP application with a database. Real work to run well. Judged, not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (70): Long lived project, regular releases. You do the updates.
- Cost (90): Free to run, you pay for the server.
- Data control (100): Files stay on your server.
- Integration depth (40): Through a synced folder only.
- Sources: https://nextcloud.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Plain synced folder**

- Fit (55): Any sync tool that puts files on the server works. No permissions model beyond the tags.
- Setup effort (90): Point KNOWLEDGE_DIR at the folder.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Plain files, nothing to keep running.
- Cost (100): Free. Judged from its description.
- Data control (100): Stays where you put it.
- Integration depth (100): Read directly. Judged from its description.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/lorefern (checked this repo)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** If the company files already live in Google Drive, copy the folders that matter into the company folder template and let Lorefern read that. It is the simplest and safest start.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** The Drive adapter is read only and was tested against a local stand in only. Use a service account limited to one folder, and read doc 13 first: Drive sharing rules are not copied into Lorefern.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** A synced plain folder costs nothing. Nextcloud is open source and costs a small server.
- **When open source is the right call:** Open source storage is the right call when files must stay on a server you control. It is the wrong call for a team that already shares everything in Drive.

### Team chat (read from an export)

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

What Lorefern has for each: Slack: Export reader (folder or zip) tested on a made up export. Layout UNVERIFIED (not run against a real export); Mattermost: No reader (not run); Zulip: No reader (not run).

**Evidence, Slack**

- Fit (70): Decisions often live in channels. Lorefern reads channel files as documents.
- Setup effort (60): Exports are a feature of the workspace plan and owner role. Plan limits not checked.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): Mature service. The export layout can change.
- Cost (50): Seat pricing. No figures quoted.
- Data control (45): Data sits with the vendor. Channel tags are set by you, not copied from Slack.
- Integration depth (40): Messages only. Threads, files and edits are not rebuilt.
- Sources: https://slack.com/help/articles/201658943-Export-your-workspace-data (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Mattermost**

- Fit (65): Self hosted team chat with a similar shape to Slack.
- Setup effort (50): Needs a server and a database. Judged, not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): Established open core project. You do the updates.
- Cost (85): A free edition exists. Paid editions have their own page.
- Data control (100): Messages stay on your server.
- Integration depth (0): No reader here. Use the recipe prompts to have Claude Code or Codex write one.
- Sources: https://mattermost.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Zulip**

- Fit (60): Topic based open source chat. Good for long running threads.
- Setup effort (50): Needs a server. Judged, not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): Active project. You do the updates.
- Cost (85): Free to self host. A hosted plan has its own page.
- Data control (100): Messages stay on your server.
- Integration depth (0): No reader here. Judged from its description.
- Sources: https://zulip.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Skip chat at first. Add a Slack export later, one public channel at a time, and map each channel to a visibility tag.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Lorefern reads a Slack export folder or zip. The layout was written from memory and is UNVERIFIED against a real export, so test it on the client's own export before promising anything. Never import private channels or direct messages without the owner's written yes.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** A one off export costs nothing. Mattermost and Zulip are open source chat tools, but Lorefern has no reader for their exports.
- **When open source is the right call:** Open source chat is the right call when messages must stay on your own server. It is the wrong call when the team already uses Slack and will not move.

- Reliability and upkeep (95): Nothing to keep running.
- Cost (100): Free. Judged from its description.

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Paste a transcript on the Meetings page, or put transcript files in a folder. That needs no recorder account at all.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Fireflies and Fathom adapters were written from their own current API docs and tested against local stand ins only. Meetily is open source and local, but its free edition names no export format, so use its transcript as a text file. Otter's export layout could not be read.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** Pasting text is free. Meetily is free software that runs on your own computer. Recorders have their own plans, read each price page yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** Meetily is the right call when audio must never leave the laptop. It is the wrong call when a team needs a bot that joins calls and shares notes by default.

### Search index for the knowledge base

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone) | paid | 85 | 55 | 85 | 40 | 40 | 0 | **60.8** | reference |
| SQLite full text (FTS5) | open_source | 60 | 95 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **83.8** | 71 percent of Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone) |
| Postgres full text | open_source | 60 | 80 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 90 | **80.5** | 71 percent of Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone) |
| pgvector (Postgres extension) | open_source | 80 | 50 | 75 | 95 | 100 | 0 | **71.0** | 94 percent of Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone) |

What Lorefern has for each: Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone): Not built. Lorefern uses a hashed word vector stand in (not run); SQLite full text (FTS5): Built and tested (run in the tests and the demo); Postgres full text: Built, SQL path exercised in a throwaway Postgres 17 (run in a local test); pgvector (Postgres extension): Not built. Not installed in the local Postgres used here (not run).

**Evidence, Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone)**

- Fit (85): Meaning based search finds pages that share no words with the question, which is the weakness measured in this repo.
- Setup effort (55): Needs an account, an index and a way to make embeddings.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Managed service. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (40): Usage priced. Not read today.
- Data control (40): Documents and vectors leave your server.
- Integration depth (0): No adapter exists in Lorefern.
- Sources: https://docs.pinecone.io/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, SQLite full text (FTS5)**

- Fit (60): Word matching with ranking. Misses questions that use other words than the page, as the held out set shows.
- Setup effort (95): Ships inside Python, nothing to install.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Very stable, runs in one file.
- Cost (100): Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Data control (100): Data stays in your database file.
- Integration depth (100): Used directly, with a rebuild step.
- Sources: https://www.sqlite.org/fts5.html (checked 2026-11-23 (BM25 and MATCH used as documented))

**Evidence, Postgres full text**

- Fit (60): Same word matching idea as SQLite, with stemming rules of its own.
- Setup effort (80): Already there when the client runs Postgres.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Stable and widely run. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (100): Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Data control (100): Stays in your database. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Integration depth (90): Lorefern stores stems and queries them with to_tsvector.
- Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, pgvector (Postgres extension)**

- Fit (80): Would allow meaning based search inside Postgres if embeddings are produced elsewhere.
- Setup effort (50): Needs the extension on the host. Not present in the local Postgres 17 used for tests, and host support is UNVERIFIED.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): Well known extension. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (95): Free, plus embedding costs.
- Data control (100): Stays in your database. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Integration depth (0): No adapter exists in Lorefern.
- Sources: https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector (checked not fetched)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Keep the built in SQLite search for a demo and for a small company. You do not need to set up anything else.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Use SQLite full text for a single client on one server, Postgres full text when the client runs on Postgres. Add real embeddings only after you measure that keyword search misses too many questions (the held out numbers in this repo show it does for wording that differs from the pages).
- **Cost sensitive owner:** Both full text options cost nothing extra. A hosted vector database adds a monthly bill and a second place your data lives.
- **When open source is the right call:** Open source search is the right call for a company knowledge base of a few thousand pages. A hosted vector database is worth it when meaning based search over a large, changing set matters more than cost.

### Who writes the answer sentences

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Language model (Anthropic API) | paid | 90 | 60 | 85 | 50 | 50 | 40 | **69.8** | reference |
| Offline rules writer (built in) | open_source | 40 | 100 | 95 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **78.2** | 44 percent of Language model (Anthropic API) |

What Lorefern has for each: Language model (Anthropic API): Plug in written against the base wrapper, never run (not run); Offline rules writer (built in): Built and tested (run in the tests and the demo).

**Evidence, Language model (Anthropic API)**

- Fit (90): Can phrase one answer from several pages and handle other wording and languages, which the offline writer cannot.
- Setup effort (60): Needs an API key. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Hosted service with limits.
- Cost (50): Priced per token. Not read today.
- Data control (50): Document text and questions would leave the server, wrapped as untrusted data. No model is wired in yet.
- Integration depth (40): The writer interface exists and the groundedness check judges its output. Never run live.
- Sources: https://docs.anthropic.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Offline rules writer (built in)**

- Fit (40): Copies the best source sentences. First run on the held out set: see docs/ANSWER-EVAL.md, it is weak on different wording.
- Setup effort (100): Nothing to set up. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Reliability and upkeep (95): Deterministic, same input same output.
- Cost (100): Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Data control (100): Nothing leaves the server.
- Integration depth (100): Built in. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Sources: data/eval/heldout_first_run.json (checked 2026-11-23 (our own first run numbers))

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Use the offline rules writer to try the product. It copies sentences from your pages, which is dull but never invents anything.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Measure before you switch: run the held out questions and the test cases with the model writer in a test account, and keep the groundedness check on whatever writes the words.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** The offline writer costs nothing. A model writer costs per use. Read the price page yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** There is no open source model scored here. Self hosted models are possible but were not tried.

### Where Lorefern stores its data

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | open_source | 90 | 65 | 95 | 85 | 95 | 90 | **86.8** | reference |
| SQLite | open_source | 60 | 100 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **84.5** | 67 percent of PostgreSQL |

What Lorefern has for each: PostgreSQL: Migrations run up, down and up again on a throwaway cluster (run in a local test); SQLite: Built and tested. The default (run in the tests and the demo).

**Evidence, PostgreSQL**

- Fit (90): Handles many readers and writers and has managed hosting almost everywhere.
- Setup effort (65): Needs a server or a managed plan.
- Reliability and upkeep (95): Very mature. Judged from its description.
- Cost (85): Free software. Hosting costs apply.
- Data control (95): You choose where it runs.
- Integration depth (90): Full migration path is tested.
- Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, SQLite**

- Fit (60): One file. Fine for a trial and a very small company. One writer at a time.
- Setup effort (100): Nothing to set up. Judged from its description.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Solid, but a single file must be backed up with care.
- Cost (100): Free. Judged from its description.
- Data control (100): A file on your disk. Judged from its description.
- Integration depth (100): Everything in this repo runs on it.
- Sources: https://www.sqlite.org/docs.html (checked not fetched)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Leave the default SQLite file for the demo and a small trial. It needs nothing.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Use Postgres for a real install so several people can work at once and backups are routine. The migration cycle was run on a throwaway Postgres 17. The search path on Postgres was not measured for answer quality.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** SQLite costs nothing. Postgres is a line on your hosting bill.
- **When open source is the right call:** Both are open source. Pick Postgres when you need more than one writer or managed backups.

- Data control (85): You choose the region and hold the data.
- Integration depth (75): Compose file, Caddyfile, backup script and cloud init are in the repo. Not run.
- Sources: https://docs.hetzner.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Vercel for the web part and Railway for the API and worker is the least work.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Hetzner with Docker Compose when you run several clients and want one bill and full control. Keep the web on Vercel if you like preview deploys.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** A small Hetzner server is the cheapest for the API. Check current prices yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** Self hosting is the right call when data must stay in one place you control. It costs your time for updates and backups.

### Named but not scored

- Any SMTP email service: Reminders are sent through plain SMTP after another person approves. It was tested against a local stand in only. Any provider that offers SMTP works the same way.
- Anthropic API (see the answer writer group): Scored there as the model option.
- Gmail, Outlook, Teams, Zoom and other tools: No adapter. Use the recipe prompts to have Claude Code or Codex write one.

<!-- SCORES:END -->

## How to read the scores

Fit counts for 35 percent, setup effort 15, reliability and upkeep 15, cost 15, data control 10 and integration depth 10. Closeness is an alternative's fit divided by the paid reference's fit. Integration depth is how much of the tool Lorefern actually uses today, so a good open source tool with no adapter scores low there on purpose. The method is described in the shared comparison method of the Sendora systems.
